sentences.text: The hare turned white seven days before the snow, every year, and had done for longer than anybody could account for.
This was not a story in Bjørnstad.
It was not told at parties or written on anything.

It was the sort of fact that a place keeps in the same drawer as the date the water gets turned off and which side of the church the ice comes in on — dull, useful, and known by everybody in a way that meant nobody explained it.
The hare lived on the slope above the last houses.
There was only ever one.
When one died another was there the following spring, which people accepted without much comment, in the way you accept that there is always a robin in the churchyard.

And in October or November — it moved about, which was the whole point of the thing — the hare would come down onto the lower ground one morning with its coat gone from brown to white, and everybody in the village would look at it and go home and do the seven days' work.
The seven days' work was specific.
You brought the outside animals down.
You lifted whatever was still in the ground, potatoes especially, because potatoes in frozen ground are potatoes you have lost.
You got the winter wood stacked under the eave and not merely stacked.
You put the boards over the pump.

You did the thing with the pipe under the Hansens' bridge that nobody could explain the reason for but which had been done every year since 1938 and which the year it was not done, in 1971, had cost the village a great deal of money.
Seven days was exactly enough time if you started on the first day.
Marit's grandfather had done the sums once, on the back of a feed bag, in about 1980, and the feed bag had been kept.
Two people, seven days, working evenings and the whole of a weekend, came out at just over the total.
Not comfortably over.
Over by about half a day, which meant that a broken pump or a sick cow or somebody's back going ate the margin entirely.
That was why the seven days was a village thing and not a household thing.
Nobody in Bjørnstad got their own potatoes up.

Everybody got everybody's potatoes up, in a rolling order that had been settled some time before the war and that was never discussed, and if you were new you were told the order once and then never again.
The Hansens went first because they were oldest.
The top houses went last because they had the pump and the pump had to be done anyway.
You did not thank anyone.
Marit had once, at nine, thanked Kristian's mother for coming, and had been looked at in a way that stopped her doing it again.
It was not enough time if you started on the third.
The year they started on the third was 1971, and it is the only year anybody in Bjørnstad ever refers to by its number.
What happened in 1971 was not dramatic and that is exactly why it is remembered.
The hare turned on the ninth of November.

A man called Sverre, who had come from Bergen two years earlier and who was by all accounts perfectly capable, was at that time renting the mill house and had responsibility for the stretch of pipe under the Hansens' bridge.
He did not do the thing with the pipe.
He did not refuse to do it.

He simply did not know it was his, because the man who had told him the order had told him once, at a wedding, and had not mentioned the pipe, because the pipe was not part of the order — the pipe was just a thing the mill house did.

The pipe froze and split on the second night of the snow and the water went under the Hansens' bridge instead of through it, and the bridge came off its abutment in the January thaw, and the village was seventeen months and a great deal of money getting a new one.
Nobody blamed Sverre.
Marit has checked this with three separate people who were adults at the time and they all say the same thing with some force: nobody blamed Sverre, Sverre was fine, Sverre was told wrong.
What the village blamed was the telling.
And from 1972 there was a list, typed, on the wall of the co-op, with everything on it including the pipe, and it is still there, and it has been retyped twice.
